Objective: Decide whether we commit to a company-wide rollout of the field diagnostic copilot, and if so, on what evidentiary and ownership basis — not to bless a schedule that already exists.

Body: The process in scope is **field repair diagnosis and escalation** — starts when a technician opens a work order in the FSM system, ends when the repair is verified and logged back into that same system. Today this process has no single accountable owner. I will not sign off a company-wide date until someone with budget authority claims all three ownership tests: authority to change technician workflow, a budget that carries the benefit, and accountability when a wrong diagnosis reaches a customer. My working assumption is the Field Operations VP is the right candidate [ASSUMPTION: based on org chart, needs confirmation they hold FSM budget].

Cost of the current process: unknown. We have a pilot productivity number, not a business case. Value Realization Lead and Finance should rerun the pilot data against the labor, parts, and downtime costs actually tracked in the FSM system's standard reporting — not the pilot's own instrumentation — and state explicitly whether the projected payback assumes headcount reduction. If it does, that goes in the executive summary in those words, not "productivity gains."

Explicitly out of scope for this first phase: the disputed-diagnosis case. This is the hard exception, and it is currently unowned — no process map, no escalation path, no override authority. Until Field Ops VP and senior technician representatives co-design who can override the copilot, on what evidence, and how that override is logged, this exception falls to whatever the technician does informally today — precisely the resistance we're seeing. Resistance here is information, not noise: technicians overriding a wrong diagnosis have reasons, and treating that as change-management friction rather than design input is how these programmes fail.

Concrete leads and first actions:
- **Escalation design** — Field Ops VP + 3–4 senior technicians. Target: one-page process map with named override authority in two weeks, with a checkpoint at one week to assess whether resistance means that target needs to move.
- **Value case** — Value Realization Lead + Finance rebase pilot numbers against FSM-reported cost data, state the headcount assumption plainly.
- **Data/model** — Data lead validates a golden dataset from repair logs, documents known defects, no further training until signed off.
- **Architecture/integration** — Technology lead brings target architecture and FSM integration blueprint to a decision meeting within three weeks; no vendor commitment before that.
- **Compliance** — Legal/Risk determines AI Act applicability within two weeks; bias/model risk review completes within four weeks, on a fixed calendar date, not "before scale" language that a slipping schedule can quietly absorb.
- **Resourcing** — Program Lead audits resource plans across all workstreams within one week to confirm which are actually unresourced (readiness assessment is my current guess, not a confirmed finding), then assigns a named owner with a two-week deadline to produce a resourcing plan.

Approach: pause the milestone date. Resume only once an owner is named, the value case uses FSM-reported cost data, the escalation process is mapped, and Legal has answered the AI Act question.

Citations: https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/high-level-summary/ (high-risk classification relevant to safety-critical guidance systems); https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework (model risk and bias audit approach).

Risks: No named owner exists today — proceeding without one means the rollout leans on authority nobody actually holds. The payback figure may assume headcount reduction that hasn't been said out loud to the technicians affected. Technician and line-manager resistance is a signal about trust and loss of diagnostic discretion, not a training gap. The disputed-diagnosis exception, if left unmapped, will surface in the field within weeks of scale, not in a review meeting. The bias/model risk review, without a fixed date, could be quietly overtaken by a de facto go-live — it now has one. The resourcing gap has been assumed, not confirmed, and assigning an owner to the wrong gap wastes a week we don't have. AI Act status is unresolved for a safety-critical system, which is legal exposure, not a paperwork item. The timeline is already behind an unvalidated plan; committing to a new date now would repeat the same mistake.

Next Steps: Field Operations VP confirms in writing within one week whether they accept ownership under the three tests above. If yes, they co-lead the escalation map with technician representatives, target two weeks, checkpoint at one. Program Lead completes the resource-plan audit within one week and names an owner for the confirmed gap. Value Realization Lead reruns the business case against FSM-reported costs before any date is proposed. Legal delivers the AI Act determination within two weeks and completes the bias/model risk review within four. I will not sign off a rollout date until these five land.
